idiom_name: sealed trait + case classes, operations as match functions (or folds)
implementation_notes: Scala's idiom is the algebraic data type: a sealed trait with case classes as variants, and each operation a function that matches on it, with the compiler warning when a match is not exhaustive. The maintenance economics are the same trade Visitor makes - data fixed, operations open - but without two hierarchies and an accept() per element, which is why Odersky calls the visitor pattern 'very bulky' in Scala and prefers pattern matching. When the representation must stay hidden, the same idea reappears as an internal visitor or fold shipped with the type (circe's Folder is the documented case), so users still add operations while the case classes stay private. Keep the visitor trait form for hierarchies that must remain open to external extension, which a sealed trait forbids by construction.
code_sketch:
sealed trait Expr
case class Num(value: Double) extends Expr
case class Add(left: Expr, right: Expr) extends Expr

def evaluate(e: Expr): Double = e match {     // warning if non-exhaustive
  case Num(v)    => v
  case Add(l, r) => evaluate(l) + evaluate(r)
}
// def render(e: Expr): String = e match { ... }   // a new operation, new function
pitfalls: Non-exhaustive matches are warnings and MatchError is a runtime failure; turn warnings into errors in CI (-Xfatal-warnings / -Werror) or the guarantee is advisory.
sealed is not transitive: matching on a subtype that is not itself sealed loses the check, and `final` classes do not get exhaustiveness checking either.
Case classes give value equality and copy, so visitors that accumulate state must not be stored inside the immutable tree.
Guards and extractors can defeat exhaustiveness: a guarded case before a general one shadows it, and custom extractors remove the compiler's ability to prove coverage.

variants.name: Visitor trait with accept(), the literal GoF translation
variants.idiom_name: trait Visitor with visit() plus accept(visitor) on elements
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF structure written in Scala: a Visitor trait with one visit method (overloaded or matching internally), and elements implementing accept(visitor) = visitor.visit(this). It is occasionally warranted when the element hierarchy cannot be sealed because library users must add variants, when the operation must be a configured object selected at runtime (a singleton stateless visitor or one instance per traversal), or when interop with Java visitors is required. Expect more code and weaker checking than the sealed-trait match: implementations of the trait are complete by construction, but nothing enumerates the element set, and a match inside visit reintroduces the dispatch the trait was added for.
pitfalls: Mixing the trait form with a match inside visit keeps both dispatch mechanisms: pick one and delete the other.
Stateful visitors must be instantiated per traversal; a singleton object with mutable state is shared mutable state across threads.
In Scala 2, overloading visit for element subtypes can make inference pick the base trait at the call site; annotate parameter types explicitly.
Trait-based visitors compile to an extra indirection per element, and the JVM does not inline megamorphic call sites - pattern matching on sealed traits is measurably faster in tight loops.
